Neonates of the Mary River turtle emerge from their incubating eggs with a carapace length of 3 centimeters [Lb = 3 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to each embryonated egg. The incubation period itself is strongly temperature-dependent; when maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], eggs hatch after 56 days [ab = 56 days], a duration that aligns with the relatively protracted developmental schedules observed among chelid turtles of comparable egg size. This thermal sensitivity during early ontogeny has important consequences for the phenology of nest emergence, as hatchlings that emerge later in the austral summer face reduced time for foraging and growth before entering their first winter dormancy. Field observations indicate that the small carapace length at birth likely constrains the types of prey items juveniles can handle, contributing to a diet dominated by aquatic insect larvae and small mollusks during the first few years of life. The energetic cost of producing relatively large, yolk-rich eggs is substantial for gravid females, and this initial investment is reflected in the tight relationship between maternal body size and clutch characteristics documented in the species. Hatchlings begin exogenous feeding within a few days of eclosion, preying upon zooplankton and small crustaceans.

As juvenile individuals grow, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before attaining reproductive maturity. Under the thermal regime typical of their natural habitat, approximately 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time since birth at puberty for both sexes is approximately 15 years [tp = approximately 15 years], a value that underscores the extremely delayed maturation characteristic of this long-lived species. Interestingly, males tend to reach puberty at a slightly smaller body size, with puberty occurring at a carapace length of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters], whereas females typically do not initiate gonadal activation until they reach approximately 29 centimeters [Lp = approximately 29 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is common among chelonians and likely reflects the greater abdominal volume required by females to accommodate developing egg clutches. The delay in female maturation relative to body size has implications for population dynamics, as it prolongs the pre-reproductive period and reduces the effective number of breeding females in the population at any given time. Growth trajectories from mark-recapture studies confirm that individuals exhibit indeterminate growth, though annual increments slow considerably after the onset of sexual maturity, with resources increasingly diverted toward gametogenesis and egg production rather than continued linear expansion.

Adult females reach an ultimate carapace length of 31.72 centimeters [Li = 31.72 centimeters], whereas males, the larger sex in this species, attain a maximum of 37.47 centimeters [Li = 37.47 centimeters] — a reversal of the typical chelonian pattern of female-biased size dimorphism distinctive to the Mary River turtle, hypothesized to relate to male-male competition for access to nesting females. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to these asymptotic dimensions is considerable, with the largest individuals reaching 3800 grams [Wwi = 3800 grams], a body mass that places Elusor macrurus among the heavier members of the Chelidae. Maintaining such a large body mass requires substantial food intake, and the species is known to consume a varied diet including aquatic vegetation, fruits fallen into the water, and occasional carrion. The energetic demands of sustaining a large adult body are also reflected in the species' relatively low fecundity, as resources must be partitioned between continued slow growth, maintenance of body condition, and reproductive effort. Comparative data from related species suggest that the large size of males may confer an advantage in securing high-quality basking sites and prime foraging territories along the riverbanks.

Under the thermal conditions of their natural riverine environment, maintained at approximately 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum lifespan documented for the species is 30 years [am = 30 years], a longevity that is moderate among freshwater turtles but notable given the relatively high metabolic demands of a warm-water habitat. Individuals that survive to this advanced age exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, with clutch sizes declining in the oldest females. The protracted lifespan is coupled with a very low annual reproductive output; females produce an average of 14.7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 14.7 eggs per clutch] and typically deposit only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. This single-clutch-per-year schedule is likely constrained by the short austral summer window available for successful incubation and hatchling emergence before winter temperatures render foraging conditions unfavorable. The combination of delayed maturity, modest clutch size, and infrequent reproduction makes the Mary River turtle particularly vulnerable to population declines from adult mortality, whether from predation, habitat degradation, or incidental capture in fishing gear. Conservation efforts have therefore focused on protecting adult females during their overland nesting migrations.

The reproductive rate at a carapace length of 24.6 centimeters, a size that corresponds to young adult females early in their reproductive careers, has been estimated at 14.7 eggs per year, reflecting the product of clutch size and the single annual nesting event under the prevailing temperature conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This modest annual output is typical of the Australian chelid fauna, many of which exhibit K-selected life-history strategies characterized by slow growth, late maturation, and extended reproductive lifespans. The species' riverine habitat in southeastern Queensland is subject to seasonal flooding and drought cycles, and females time their nesting migrations to coincide with favorable sandbank conditions. Nest site selection is critical for egg survival, as temperatures above 30 °C can cause embryonic mortality, while cooler, waterlogged nests delay hatching or promote fungal infection. The persistence of Elusor macrurus populations will depend on maintaining the thermal integrity of their nesting beaches and ensuring that adult females can safely complete their annual migrations. Ongoing monitoring programs continue to refine estimates of age-specific fecundity and survival, providing the demographic data needed to assess population viability under various climate scenarios and to prioritize areas for habitat protection and restoration efforts.
